description: Sabotages for the ntdll inline-hook facility in src/trace/hook.rs -- the stub recogniser that makes patching safe, the trampoline that rebuilds the displaced system call, and the table column that decides which calls carry a worker factory handle. Run with tools/run-sabotage.ps1; see tools/README-sabotage.md for the format and for why the results are read the way they are.
coveredSinceM-T10.5: The hook trampoline's own `-enter` and `-leave` records ARE swept, by the two entries below. They were not, and could not be, until M-T10.5: the assertions existed but sat behind `if wants("wfactory")`, and neither this harness nor CI sets WINDOWS_THREADPOOL_TRACE, so a sabotage deleting those `record` calls was scored SURVIVED against a guard that did exist. The fix was to run the test body in a trace-armed child via trace::in_a_trace_armed_child, which fixes the filter before `main` the only way a test can. Both sabotages are caught by name rather than by a crash. An earlier version of this note cited M-T4.1 for the outstanding work, which is a completed decision about the name of the synchronous close and never covered it -- so the job was, in practice, queued nowhere.
notCoveredHere: The hook module's OTHER records are still absent, and for a different reason than the two above: no test asserts them at all, so there is nothing here to make reachable. They are `installed` / `refused` / `refused-after-seal` from the install path, `factory-found` / `factories-seen` / the `counts-*` family from the worker-factory probe, `port-depth` / `ports-seen` / `port-unavailable` / `port-poking` / `port-poked` from the completion-port scan, and `associate-already-signalled` from the wait-registration hook. Each has a test that exercises the code emitting it, but every one of those tests asserts the VALUE the function returns rather than the record it writes -- `the_factory_scan_finds_the_pool_and_reads_plausible_counts` checks the counts, `the_port_scan_finds_a_completion_port_and_reads_its_depth` checks the depth, and `hooking_the_wait_registration_observes_the_already_signalled_flag` deliberately asserts only that the hook fired, because which flag value comes back is a fact about the kernel on the day. So deleting any of those `record` calls would be reported SURVIVED, correctly: the guard really is missing. Queued as M-T10.36 in CHECKLIST.md.
whyTestArgs: --all-features, because the whole hook module is behind the `trace` feature. Without it the module is not compiled, every sabotage lands in code that does not exist, and the sweep reports SURVIVED for guards that are present and working.

sabotages.name: the trampoline omits the system call
sabotages.why: The trampoline rebuilds the displaced stub from the system call number. Replacing the two-byte `syscall` with NOPs leaves a trampoline that returns whatever was in eax without entering the kernel, so the hooked call silently stops doing anything. This is the failure that would make every hooked measurement a fiction while the process kept running, so the guard has to notice it by the call's own results rather than by a crash.

sabotages.name: the recogniser accepts anything
sabotages.why: The recogniser is the entire safety argument for patching another module's code: it is what stops a jump being planted over instructions nobody decoded. A version that returns true unconditionally would happily corrupt any export whose name resolved.

sabotages.name: the recogniser pins the system call number
sabotages.why: The four system-call-number bytes are the one part of the stub that legitimately varies, between functions and between Windows builds. A recogniser that matched them too would refuse every stub but the one it was written against -- a failure that looks like safety and is in fact a facility that never works. This is the opposite direction from the sabotage above, and a guard that only tested one of them would pass either way.

sabotages.name: an unknown hook label falls back to the first entry
sabotages.why: A typo in WINDOWS_THREADPOOL_TRACE_HOOKS must refuse, not silently patch whichever stub happens to be first in the table. The first entry is the worker park, the hottest path in the pool, so this mistake would be both invisible and maximally perturbing.
find: let Some(index) = HOOKS.iter().position(|(_, name, _)| *name == label) else {

sabotages.name: the fired counter never increments
sabotages.why: The counter is what makes the facility's guard run on a machine with no trace environment set. Removing the increment is indistinguishable, to every unconditional assertion, from a jump that was never planted -- which is exactly the state the guard exists to rule out.

sabotages.name: every hooked call is taken to carry a factory handle
sabotages.why: Only the worker-factory calls have a factory handle in their first argument. Ignoring the table column that says so lets a stub with an out-pointer there install itself as the handle, after which the factory counters describe whatever that pointer was -- an error that reports itself as a plain query failure and would be read as the factory's own answer. This sabotage is here because the defect was real: it was in the first draft of the module and was caught while writing the table, not by a test.

sabotages.name: the factory layout is the wrong size
sabotages.why: The query rejects a buffer whose length does not match the information class, so a struct that is the wrong SIZE fails every call while looking exactly like a process that has no worker factory. This defect was real -- it was the first draft, and it made the scan report nothing on a machine where the scan works. Padding the struct reproduces it: `_tail` has no readers, so the size changes and nothing else does.
sabotages.whyNotTruncation: This case used to DELETE the five fields from `start_routine` to `stack_commit`, which was the original defect's own shape. That stopped working on 2026-10-01: those fields acquired readers when the factory snapshot began emitting them, so the patch became a compile error (E0609, five times) instead of the runtime failure it is meant to produce, and the harness reported MANIFEST DOES NOT COMPILE. Checked before repairing, per M-T6.9: the patch was not being caught by a const assertion, which would have meant re-declaring the case rather than repairing it. Growing the struct through a field nothing reads produces the same wrong size with no such coupling.

sabotages.name: the handle scan gives up immediately
sabotages.why: The scan is what makes the factory readable in a stalled process, where no hooked call has fired and so no handle has been learned. A ceiling that stops before any real handle leaves it finding nothing, which is indistinguishable from a process with no pool -- and would have been read as exactly that.
find: /// this is generous for a test process rather than a tuned figure.
replace: /// this is generous for a test process rather than a tuned figure.

sabotages.name: the pre-main initialiser is dropped by the linker
sabotages.why: `#[used]` is what stops the linker discarding a static nothing references, and `.CRT$XCU` is what makes the CRT call it before main. Getting either wrong still builds: the instrument silently reverts to installing hooks lazily, which in the investigation this was built for lands 0.12s into the process, long after the fault is established. Renaming the section reproduces exactly that -- a working build whose initialiser never runs.

sabotages.name: the suspended window allocates
sabotages.why: A DELIBERATE control, and the one entry here that documents a hazard the tests cannot see. Dropping the reservation on `held` makes the push allocate while other threads are suspended, and a thread suspended holding the allocator lock can never give it back -- a deadlock. It survives because the tests install hooks from a process whose other threads are not holding that lock at that instant, so the defect is real and the suite is blind to it. It is recorded here so the reservation is not removed as redundant by a future reader; the argument for it is in the comment at the call site, not in a test. NOTE: this reservation was for a long time the ONLY thing guarding that window, while the install it wrapped was separately taking the allocator lock through ntdll_proc's owned name, the LOADER lock through GetModuleHandleA and GetProcAddress, and the memory manager through VirtualAlloc and VirtualProtect. A review found those; the install is now split into prepare/commit/finish and the window holds a single fourteen-byte store. The reservation still matters and this control still survives, but it is no longer the whole of the protection and must not be read as though it were.
find: let mut held: Vec<*mut core::ffi::c_void> = Vec::with_capacity(ids.len());
replace: let mut held: Vec<*mut core::ffi::c_void> = Vec::new();

sabotages.name: the wait's Drop cancels instead of draining
sabotages.why: The teardown-drains decision: Drop must run a queued callback, not discard it. This is the exact defect the M26.13 investigation measured -- the cancelling form leaves the default pool unable to make its first worker. Both forms leave the object quiescent, so only a guard asserting the callback RAN can tell them apart, which is why the tests that were already here could not.
find: // The lock is released before draining: a callback blocked on it would
// otherwise never finish, and this wait would never return.
replace: // The lock is released before draining: a callback blocked on it would
// otherwise never finish, and this wait would never return.

sabotages.name: the wait's stop_and_drain cancels instead of draining
sabotages.why: The early-discharge method a caller uses to pay the teardown cost at a point they choose. Separate from Drop because they are separate call sites: fixing one and not the other would leave whichever the caller did not reach still discarding work. The method has been named `stop_and_drain` and implemented as a cancel since it was written.

sabotages.name: the timer's disarm is taken to leave a queued tick alone
sabotages.why: Pins the asymmetry that decides whether this crate's timer teardown can distinguish draining from cancelling: SetThreadpoolTimer(NULL) discards a queued tick where SetThreadpoolWait(NULL) does not. Inverting the expectation must fail, because the whole argument for leaving the timer's drain form unverified rests on this being measured rather than assumed.

sabotages.name: CONTROL: a refusal reason is renumbered
sabotages.why: The control this manifest needs. The numeric value of a refusal reason is carried into a trace record and never compared against anything, so changing it cannot break a test. A sweep in which this were CAUGHT would mean the suite is sensitive to something other than behaviour, and the CAUGHT results above would be worth no more than this one.

sabotages.name: the repair object is closed without draining it
sabotages.why: CloseThreadpoolWork does not wait -- it frees the work object asynchronously once outstanding callbacks finish. A repair callback stamps last_started on entry, which is exactly what makes its entry retirable, and then writes to the entry again. Without the drain, a retirement landing between those two writes drops the last Arc and the callback finishes into a released allocation. The guard asserts the retirement blocked rather than waiting for a fault, because a crash-caught result is treated as uncovered here.

sabotages.name: a cancellation does not arm a repair
sabotages.why: The first of the three claims the self-heal rests on. `try_cancel_pending` is a safe method only because the crate repairs the pool the cancel may have wedged, and the repair begins with the mark. A cancel that does not mark leaves the pool to be fixed by whatever the application happens to submit next, which for a program built on waits, timers and I/O is nothing.
find: // After the stamp, never before: the healer's first tick must
replace: // After the stamp, never before: the healer's first tick must

sabotages.name: a dispatch never updates its pool's stamp
sabotages.why: The second claim. Health is derived, not stored: a pool is unhealed while its last cancellation is at or after the last time its own repair callback ran. This stamp is the only thing that ever heals an entry, so a trampoline that does not write it leaves every cancelled pool unhealed forever -- the entry is never retired, and every tick that finds no repair in flight submits another.

sabotages.name: the heal creates a work object instead of submitting the pre-created one
sabotages.why: The third claim, and the one that is easiest to break while looking correct. Creating a work object was measured NOT to release a stalled pool; only submitting one is. So the repair object is made when the pool is registered, and the healing path must do nothing but submit it. The patch below still submits something, and on a real pool would still release the stall -- which is why the guard is tied to the entry's OWN repair object through its callback context, not to a count of repairs in general.
sabotages.whyNotNullContext: The fresh object is given its own valid counter rather than a null context. With null the trampoline dereferences it and the process aborts, which the harness scores as caught -- but by a crash, not by a test noticing, and this repository treats a crash-caught mutant as an uncovered one.

sabotages.name: the hook records entering the call but the record is dropped
sabotages.why: Half of what a hook is for. A trampoline that performs the displaced system call correctly but records nothing leaves an investigation reading an empty capture and concluding the call never happened -- which is the exact inference this facility exists to support, so a silent hook is worse than no hook. The patch keeps the arguments live, so this is the record going missing rather than the call changing shape.
find: record(TARGET, concat!($label, "-enter"), a1 as u64, a2 as u64);

sabotages.name: the hook records leaving the call but the record is dropped
sabotages.why: The other end, and the one whose absence is hardest to read: with no `-leave` record a call that never returned is indistinguishable from one that did, so a hang and a success look alike in the capture. That is precisely the distinction the stall investigation turned on.
find: record(TARGET, concat!($label, "-leave"), a1 as u64, status as u32 as u64);

sabotages.name: a repair the pool never takes is waited on forever
sabotages.why: The suppression that stops a repair being queued on every tick is also what could hide a pool that is never going to run one. Removing the overdue test restores the behaviour M-T9.2 decided against: an in-flight repair is skipped no matter how long it has sat there, so a wedged pool is retried no further and reported never. The patch keeps the skip and deletes only the threshold, which is the shape the defect would really take -- the guard has to notice the elapsed time, not merely that a repair exists.

sabotages.name: the heal never gives up on a pool that will not be repaired
sabotages.why: The second half of the same decision: after one reattempt the crate has submitted the only action measured to release the stall, twice, and has nothing further to try. Under `fail-fast` that is a stop condition. Removing the comparison leaves a build that re-submits forever in a configuration whose entire purpose is to end the process rather than continue past a state it cannot establish is recoverable -- and it fails silently, because the retry loop looks exactly the same from outside.
sabotages.whyTheChildTest: Caught by a test that drives the state in a CHILD process and asserts on how it died, because the panic escapes the healer's `extern "system"` trampoline and aborts rather than unwinding. An in-process assertion would take the test runner with it.

sabotages.name: the teardown fail-fast panics before the drain instead of after it
sabotages.why: The ordering constraint the fail-fast is built around. Panicking before the drain unwinds past the disarm, the drain, `CloseThreadpoolWait` and the context free -- so the pool goes on watching a handle the unwinding field drop has already closed, and the queued callback is abandoned. That is the exact abandonment the feature exists to prevent, reached through the mechanism meant to prevent it, so a fail-fast placed here is worse than none at all.
sabotages.whyNotTheLateCall: This inserts an early call rather than moving the late one, so it is a single-site edit the harness can check for uniqueness. The early panic fires first, so the late call is never reached and the effect is the same as moving it.
sabotages.whyAssertionNotCrash: Caught by `the_drain_runs_before_the_panic` in tests/fail_fast_teardown.rs, which snapshots the callback count the instant the panic surfaces and asserts on it *before* joining the releasing thread. Both orderings end with the callback having run -- the leaked watch still fires it -- so only the timing separates them, and asserting after the join would let the crash from that leaked watch pre-empt the assertion and turn a precise failure into a bare abort.

sabotages.name: the teardown fail-fast never fires
sabotages.why: The rejecting direction. A fail-fast that is compiled in but never panics leaves the whole feature inert while every build and every feature-shape assertion still passes, so nothing except a test that observes the panic can tell the difference.

sabotages.name: the teardown fail-fast fires when nothing is owed
sabotages.why: The accepting direction, which is the half that usually goes untested. A fail-fast that panics on every drop satisfies every assertion that it fires when a drain is owed, while making the feature unusable: a caller who discharged the obligation correctly would still be punished for it.

sabotages.name: the obligation is recorded after the arming instead of before
sabotages.why: The ordering every armed object depends on, and the one this crate got wrong at three of eight sites before the pair was moved into a single method. Publishing the arming first opens a window in which a dispatch settles the obligation on a pool thread and is then overwritten, so an object that ran to completion claims it owes a drain -- under fail-fast a panic on a correctly-drained object, and an abort if Drop was already unwinding. The guard is in obligation::tests rather than in a pool test, because the ordering now lives at one site and that is where it can be made deterministic.

sabotages.name: Drop does not report the obligation it was left
sabotages.why: The report itself, as opposed to the fail-fast built on top of it. Removing the record leaves a Drop that still performs the blocking drain but tells nobody it had to, which is the condition the whole obligation mechanism exists to surface and is invisible to every test that only checks the program does not hang. This entry is also the control on tests/obligation_report.rs: that test spent its life early-returning when the trace filter was unset, so it passed while measuring nothing, and this sabotage is what demonstrates it now measures something.
